engine.meaning: Most of the letter is the original text, but swaps change facts: "eight quid every Saturday night" for eight dollars, "sixty cents on any quid" then "he never spends the quid" against "a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents", "the first travelling bloke" for the first travelling salesman, and an added "Bloody hell," and "scared stiff" that make the father alarmed rather than mildly concerned.
engine.sense: Many terms take the wrong sense: "a beaut deal like feeding" (beaut = excellent, for 'a good deal like'), "a beaut education", "a beaut merchant", "a beaut business man", "very, dead careful", "It is all with the bloke" for 'all with the man', "a bloody good deal" for 'a good deal'.
engine.authenticity: Word-swaps, not a voice: "beaut" stuck in for every 'good', "bloke" for every 'man' or 'fellow', and US forms left in ("no elevator in the building", "how to run an automobile", "scalawag steer").
engine.register: Level 3 wants a moderate retelling; this is the original with mechanical swaps. "Bloody hell," and "a bloody good deal" are within vulgarity 1 but out of place in a father's letter.
engine.tone: The dry fatherly lecture mostly survives because the text is mostly unchanged, but "Bloody hell, I simply mention these things" and "scared stiff" make it wobble.
engine.flow: Clunky joins: "very, dead careful", "a beaut deal like feeding his weight in corn", "sixty cents on any quid", "Bloody hell, I simply mention".
engine.variety: Leans on the same few swaps: "beaut" four times, "bloke" a dozen times, "quid" three times.
engine.essence: Recognisably the letter, with its napkin parable and Munchausen joke, but the swaps blur the money maths and the father's measured voice.

yarn.meaning: Every point kept, in order: Cambridge, the steer, sitting tight, the bottom at "a seat at the mailing desk, with eight dollars every Saturday night", "no lift in the building", the napkin parable, "a hundred and six cents", Munchausen and "my reps' bills". "like he's been carrying a sack of spuds" is colour on 'hump-shouldered'.
yarn.sense: Terms fit: "a mongrel of a bullock" for 'scalawag steer', "rolling in it and can wear it", "a skerrick of difference", "drapery business" for dry-goods, "telling porkies" for lying, "got a bit big for their boots".
yarn.authenticity: Reads like an Australian father writing: "making a mug of yourself", "never had to work for a quid", "hold down a pretty important job", "won't be heaps of use to you".
yarn.register: A moderate level-3 touch: Aussie idiom throughout without becoming a yarn, and no swearing, inside vulgarity 1.
yarn.tone: Keeps the dry, affectionate, lecturing father: "I can't hand you success off the shelf" and "It's all up to the man".
yarn.flow: Reads naturally: "Now, the bills won't break me, of course, but they'll break you unless you're dead careful. Very, very careful."
yarn.variety: Varied ("skerrick", "porkies", "rolling in it", "big for their boots"), though "bloke" and "fella" recur often.
yarn.essence: Unmistakably the merchant's letter: the steer, the elevator joke as "no lift", the napkin parable and the Munchausen line all intact.

unharnessed.meaning: All points kept, but the steer line is garbled: "feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn" makes the steer fail to fatten 'its weight in corn' instead of being fed it.
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit: "making a galah of yourself", "the old man's loaded and can wear it", "drapery trade" for dry-goods, "telling porkies", "won't be a scrap of real use".
unharnessed.authenticity: Mostly natural ("kept me mouth shut", "sure-fire", "galah"), with a few British-leaning picks ("the other lads", "out of college", "the works").
unharnessed.register: Level-3 weight: light idiom through the letter, no swearing.
unharnessed.tone: The dry fatherly lecture comes through: "Course, the bills won't send me broke, but they'll send you broke".
unharnessed.flow: Mostly smooth, but the steer sentence tangles and "there'll come a time when you start at the works when you won't" doubles 'when'.
unharnessed.essence: Clearly the original letter: Cambridge, the stamps, the napkin parable and Munchausen all there.

engine.quote: a beaut deal like feeding his weight in corn
engine.original: a good deal like feeding his weight in corn
engine.why: 'A good deal' (much) turned into 'beaut' (excellent): wrong sense.

engine.quote: with eight quid every Saturday night
engine.original: with eight dollars every Saturday night
engine.why: Changes the currency and amount in a Chicago letter.

engine.quote: sixty cents on any quid that comes to him. But a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents to a beaut business man, and he never spends the quid
engine.original: never able to realize more than sixty cents on any dollar that comes to him. But a dollar is worth one hundred and six cents to a good business man, and he never spends the dollar
engine.why: Mixes quid and dollar in one sum; the arithmetic joke breaks.

engine.quote: Bloody hell, I simply mention these things because I am scared stiff
engine.original: I simply mention these things because I am afraid
engine.why: Added swearing and alarm the measured father never shows.

engine.quote: It is all with the bloke.
engine.original: It is all with the man.
engine.why: 'The man' here means the individual; 'bloke' strains.

engine.quote: there is no elevator in the building
engine.original: there is no elevator in the building
engine.why: US 'elevator' left in while other words are swapped.

engine.quote: Starting, as you do, with a beaut education
engine.original: Starting, as you do, with a good education
engine.why: 'Beaut' leaned on for every 'good', always in the wrong sense.

yarn.quote: won't be heaps of use to you
yarn.original: isn't going to be of any real use to you
yarn.why: 'Heaps of use' is a slightly awkward fit for 'any real use'.

yarn.quote: it's enough to make a bloke hunch over like he's been carrying a sack of spuds
yarn.original: it fairly makes a fellow hump-shouldered to look it over
yarn.why: Colour that slightly loses 'to look it over'.

unharnessed.quote: feeding a mongrel steer that won't fatten up its own weight in corn
unharnessed.original: feeding his weight in corn to a scalawag steer that won't fat up
unharnessed.why: Reordered so the steer 'fattens up its weight in corn'; the image no longer parses.

unharnessed.quote: the other lads at the desk
unharnessed.original: the other boys at the desk

unharnessed.quote: there'll come a time when you start at the works when you won't be able
unharnessed.original: there's going to be a time when you begin at the factory when you won't be able

summaries.engine: A mechanical word-swap of the original: 'beaut' and 'bloke' everywhere, money garbled into quid, and swearing the letter does not need.
summaries.yarn: Faithful, natural, level-3 Aussie letter that keeps the father's voice and every point.
summaries.unharnessed: Natural, faithful level-3 version; one tangled sentence and a couple of British-leaning words.
